schema_notes.risk_horizon: Near Term | Medium Term | Long Term
schema_notes.who_it_affects: Workers | Households | Small Businesses | Creators & IP Holders | Global South | AI Developers | Firms | AI Infrastructure Providers | Public Institutions
schema_notes.decision_maker: Legislators | Regulatory Agencies | Multilateral Bodies | Courts | Private Actors
schema_notes.categories: Public & Social Investments | Labor Market Adaptation | Wealth Capture | Regulation & Market Design | Global Coordination

policies.title: Sectoral Subsidies
policies.summary: Public investment in sectors delivering public value and supporting employment.
policies.core_mechanism: Sustained public investments maintaining economic activity in sectors delivering public value (education, healthcare, elder care, environmental protection) through direct grants, procurement contracts, price supports, insurance programs, subsidized lending, loan guarantees, and tax incentives.
pros: Shapes economy toward high-value sectors
Prevents underprovision of socially valuable work
Creates employment in care and public services
Generates fiscal returns
Supports labor force participation
Leverages government purchasing power to steer technology adoption
cons: Risk of entrenching inefficiency without competitive pressure
Vulnerable to political lobbying over genuine need
Benefits may flow to incumbent firms rather than workers
Significant fiscal costs competing with alternative investments
Requires difficult government judgments about sector selection
precedents: US Medicare/Medicaid spending exceeds $1.5 trillion annually sustaining healthcare jobs
US K-12 education spending near $1 trillion yearly supporting 3+ million teachers
China used subsidies to dominate EV and solar manufacturing
EU Common Agricultural Policy distributes €55 billion annually for agricultural support

policies.title: Employer Tax Breaks
policies.summary: Fiscal incentives for employers who invest in retraining or hire displaced workers.
policies.core_mechanism: Tax breaks (credits or deductions) incentivize firms to invest in worker retraining, hire displaced workers, or adopt labor-augmenting AI rather than labor-replacing automation. They reform tax code asymmetries that currently favor physical capital and software investments over human capital development.
pros: Operates through existing fiscal infrastructure avoiding annual appropriations battles
Politically durable and administratively scalable
Addresses structural tax code asymmetries favoring automation
Can incentivize three behaviors simultaneously
cons: Disproportionately benefits already-profitable firms with sufficient tax liability
Provides little support to loss-making or crisis-hit firms
Risks deadweight loss from firms claiming credits for training they would undertake anyway
Poor targeting reduces cost-effectiveness
precedents: U.S. Work Opportunity Tax Credit for designated disadvantaged groups (IRS)
Georgia's Retraining Tax Credit up to $1,250 per employee annually
Rhode Island's Qualified Jobs Tax Credit up to $7,500 per new job
Singapore's Enterprise Innovation Scheme with 400% deductions on training expenditures

policies.title: AI Infrastructural Investments
policies.summary: Government funding for compute infrastructure or energy to increase competitiveness or democratize AI access.
policies.core_mechanism: Public investment in compute clusters, data centers, and clean energy to bridge the capital expenditure gap, treating AI infrastructure as a public good or strategic national asset while preventing capability concentration among large firms.
pros: Prevents AI concentration among vertically integrated firms
Enables smaller firms and public institutions to participate in AI economy
Distributes productivity gains
Supports Global South technological development
Creates accessible compute resources for researchers
cons: Massive capital requirements (tens of billions)
Multi-year construction timelines
Energy and permitting constraints
Public infrastructure may lag private innovation pace
Allocation decisions vulnerable to political pressure
precedents: Interstate Highway System unlocked private productivity and economic growth
Human Genome Project generated $141 return for every public dollar invested through open data access

policies.title: Unemployment Benefits
policies.summary: Modernizing unemployment insurance to expand eligibility and duration.
policies.core_mechanism: Unemployment insurance provides temporary income replacement to jobless workers through employer payroll taxes or social insurance contributions. Modernized versions could include automatic triggers tied to local unemployment rates, broader eligibility for non-traditional workers, and integration with reskilling programs to facilitate transitions during structural economic change.
pros: Provides immediate income stabilization during job loss
Automatic triggers can direct resources to affected regions
Integration with retraining shortens transition periods
Research shows modest reemployment delays during high unemployment
Denmark's model demonstrates low unemployment alongside low inequality
cons: Designed for temporary downturns, not permanent structural job elimination
Time-limited benefits may expire before reemployment
More generous benefits can delay job-seeking
Expanding eligibility to gig workers requires system redesign
Requires high taxation to finance comprehensive programs
precedents: COVID-19 CARES Act expanded UI through PUA and FPUC, covering gig workers for first time and preventing mass destitution
Denmark's flexicurity model combines flexible labor markets with two-year benefits and extensive retraining programs

policies.title: Universal Basic Services
policies.summary: Free or heavily subsidized access to essential services such as healthcare, education, housing, or transportation.
policies.core_mechanism: Public provision of essential services—healthcare, education, housing, transportation, childcare, and digital connectivity—guaranteed to all residents regardless of employment status or income level, treating them as public utilities rather than market commodities.
pros: Decouples essential services from employment, providing security during labor market disruption
More efficient than cash transfers for services with large economies of scale
Avoids inflation in essential goods markets
Treats basic needs as guaranteed rights rather than commodities
cons: Massive fiscal cost and implementation complexity requiring sustained political commitment
Paternalistic—determines needs on behalf of individuals rather than preserving choice
Risks creating two-tier systems in countries lacking strong public service traditions
Quality may lag behind private alternatives
precedents: UK National Health Service provides free comprehensive healthcare
Finland offers free university tuition, meals, and student housing
German cities experimented with free public transit
Vienna's social housing system houses 60% of residents in capped-rent public/limited-profit housing

policies.title: Job Guarantees & Public Works Programs
policies.summary: Governments functioning as an employer of last resort for all willing individuals.
policies.core_mechanism: Government commits to provide publicly funded jobs at set wages to workers unable to find private employment, directing labor toward infrastructure, environmental restoration, caregiving, and community services with collective societal value but insufficient market demand.
pros: Maintains workforce attachment and skill preservation
Addresses unmet infrastructure and care needs
Converts technological unemployment into public investment
Polling shows public preference for job guarantees over cash transfers
Preserves dignity and purpose beyond income function
cons: Requires substantial institutional capacity for design and administration
Tension between countercyclical stabilization and continuous service provision
Wage-setting challenges—too high may draw workers from private sector, too low may fail to provide adequate security
Difficulty identifying and scaling useful projects
precedents: South Africa's Presidential Employment Stimulus (2020) created over one million opportunities in underserved sectors
Works Progress Administration (1930s) employed 8.5 million people and funded infrastructure plus 40,000 artists, producing enduring cultural artifacts

policies.title: Wage Insurance
policies.summary: Temporary income supplements to displaced workers who accept reemployment at lower pay.
policies.core_mechanism: Wage insurance provides temporary income supplements to displaced workers accepting lower-paying reemployment, bridging the earnings gap. Unlike unemployment insurance that incentivizes joblessness, it subsidizes the wage decline proportionally, helping workers transition without extensive retraining.
pros: Accelerates reemployment without moral hazard
Generates additional cumulative earnings
Potentially self-financing
Addresses mid-to-late career workers unsuitable for multi-year retraining
No evidence workers accept lower-quality jobs
cons: Assumes lower-paying jobs exist
Subsidizes permanent wage decline
Provides safety net but lacks skill-building pathway
Limited take-up in real-world implementations due to administrative barriers and low awareness
precedents: U.S. Reemployment Trade Adjustment Assistance (RTAA) for workers 50+ (50% subsidy, $10k cap, terminated 2022)
Canada's Earnings Supplement Project (75% subsidy, modest positive effects)
Germany's Entgeltsicherung (50-30% subsidy, low uptake)

policies.title: Shortened Work Weeks
policies.summary: Reduced working hours to distribute work more evenly and convert productivity gains into leisure.
policies.core_mechanism: Reduce statutory full-time standards while preserving wages and benefits, allowing productivity gains from AI to translate into time dividends through labor law changes, subsidies for adopting firms, and public sector pilots.
pros: Distributes productivity gains broadly rather than concentrating wealth
Maintains employment relationships and benefit access
Enables worker retraining and civic participation
Precedent in Netherlands, Denmark, Germany showing sustainability
Four-day pilots report strong retention and productivity stability
cons: Higher per-unit labor costs may reduce competitiveness internationally
Risk of underemployment if wages not maintained
Benefits may flow disproportionately to salaried workers over hourly/shift workers
Mandatory policies may accelerate automation to offset labor costs
precedents: Netherlands, Denmark, Germany average 32.1–34.7 weekly hours (Eurostat 2023)
Germany's Kurzarbeit demonstrates social insurance supporting hours-reduction
Four-day week pilots showing organizational retention gains

policies.title: Union & Bargaining Rights
policies.summary: Strengthened collective bargaining giving workers a voice in AI adoption decisions.
policies.core_mechanism: Legal protections allowing workers to organize collectively and negotiate binding agreements with employers over wages, working conditions, job security, and workplace governance, including mandatory advance notice, joint labor-management committees, algorithmic disclosure, retraining provisions, and productivity-sharing arrangements.
pros: Workers gain formal voice in AI deployment decisions before implementation
Enables negotiation over terms including advance notice and data stewardship
Broad bargaining coverage can shape sector-wide norms
Allows workers to share productivity gains through wages, shorter hours, or profit-sharing
cons: Unionization rates declining in most advanced economies
Technology firms actively resist unionization
Risk that overly-restrictive requirements could slow beneficial automation
Firms can relocate to jurisdictions with weaker labor protections
Tension between protecting incumbent workers and enabling productivity improvements
precedents: 2023 Hollywood writers secured consent and compensation requirements for any use of digital likenesses (Brookings)
SAG-AFTRA negotiated similar protections requiring informed consent for digital replicas
ILO examined high road AI investment approaches through social dialogue (July 2025)

policies.title: Skill Gap Analyses
policies.summary: Standardized AI exposure measurement directing workforce funding where displacement data indicates greatest need.
policies.core_mechanism: Task-level measurement frameworks break occupations into component tasks, assess AI susceptibility, and identify which occupations and communities face greatest exposure to enable targeted retraining resource allocation.
pros: Enables precise identification of high-exposure tasks and communities
Directs retraining resources strategically
Allows distinguishing augmentation from automation
Reveals that high task exposure doesn't automatically mean job displacement
Supports anticipatory workforce planning
cons: Occupational data like O*NET updates infrequently relative to AI capability development
Theoretical task exposure may not translate to actual labor outcomes
Depends on job structure, regulations, and retraining availability
Requires continuous data infrastructure investment
precedents: U.S. Department of Labor's O*NET cataloging 20,000+ task statements across 900+ occupations
BLS Employment Projections incorporating AI impacts
Tennessee's AI Workforce Action Plan using MIT's Iceberg Index for county-level targeting
MIT/Oak Ridge's Project Iceberg simulating 151 million workers across 32,000 skills
Anthropic Economic Index measuring actual Claude usage patterns
North Carolina and Utah state-level analyses

policies.title: Workforce Training and Reskilling Investment
policies.summary: Tax incentives and subsidies connecting displaced workers to skills development.
policies.core_mechanism: Governments use tax breaks for firms investing in worker training, direct subsidies for employers creating trainee positions, and public funding for training infrastructure like community colleges and apprenticeships to increase accessible job-relevant training, particularly for workers whose skills are losing market value due to technological change.
pros: AI can enhance training through adaptive learning and personalized pathways
Sectoral partnership models show better wage outcomes than traditional approaches
Lifetime training credits expand accessibility
Reduces fiscal incentive for automation over retraining
cons: Most government-funded programs produce modest or negligible wage gains
Uncertainty about which skills retain value
Vulnerable workers often lack access due to income/caregiving constraints
Rapid displacement may outpace retraining capacity
Scaling proven intensive programs remains difficult
precedents: U.S. Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act funds 7,000+ providers
Project QUEST in San Antonio achieved RCT-proven long-term wage gains through wraparound support
Singapore's SkillsFuture provides lifetime training credits

policies.title: Entrepreneurship & Small Business Support
policies.summary: Expanded pathways for displaced workers to start businesses or become self-employed.
policies.core_mechanism: Self-employment assistance programs allow unemployed workers to collect benefits while starting businesses; public grants and subsidized lending for early-stage ventures; technical assistance and training through small business development centers; regulatory simplification reducing business formation barriers.
pros: Creates alternative adjustment pathways when traditional employment contracts
Expands self-employment viability beyond wealthy networks through public investment
Leverages domain expertise
AI tools reduce entrepreneurial overhead
Young firms drive disproportionate job creation
cons: Distinction between opportunity and necessity entrepreneurship—displacement may expand precarious self-employment
Lacks traditional employment benefits (health insurance, retirement, paid leave)
High failure rates and skewed returns
Not viable for all workers
Requires unequally distributed skills
precedents: Singapore's Enterprise Development Grant provides 50% co-funding with SkillsFuture training credits
Germany's KfW development bank offers subsidized loans and equity investments
Google's SBDC AI U Program funds 100,000 small businesses in AI training
Michigan's technical support initiative for SMB AI adoption

policies.title: AI Literacy Training
policies.summary: Comprehensive AI literacy embedded across all education levels.
policies.core_mechanism: AI literacy—combining knowledge, skills, and critical judgment to understand AI systems, evaluate outputs, and navigate societal implications—must be integrated across all disciplines rather than taught as a standalone subject, preparing students and workers for an AI-permeated economy while strengthening democratic participation.
pros: Prepares workforce for AI-fluent economy
Strengthens democratic understanding of algorithmic systems
Enables critical evaluation of AI outputs
Addresses educational equity through systematic curriculum integration
Supports both students and existing workers through coordinated education approaches
cons: Educational institutions cannot update curricula as rapidly as AI advances
Teacher training deficits create implementation bottlenecks
Content risks obsolescence requiring continuous updating
Poorly designed initiatives risk widening rather than narrowing educational divides between well-resourced and under-resourced schools
precedents: Estonia's ProgeTiger program (2012) achieved 99% kindergarten and 98% school participation in technology integration
Finland's 2014 curriculum revision embedded media literacy across subjects to combat disinformation, treating critical thinking as civic defense

policies.title: Lifelong Learning Programs
policies.summary: Continuous learning systems replacing traditional front-loaded education.
policies.core_mechanism: Shifts education from front-loaded model to continuous system combining financing mechanisms (personal learning accounts funded by government, employers, and individuals) and credential infrastructure (stackable micro-credentials and digital skill records) enabling workers to adapt throughout careers as AI reshapes skill requirements.
pros: Enables mid-career skill adaptation without income loss
Provides infrastructure for continuous adjustment to AI-driven skill changes
Reaches workers unable to pursue full-time education
Makes training portable across employers through recognized credentials
cons: Take-up remains low among workers most needing retraining due to time/financial constraints
Quality assurance challenges distinguishing credible offerings
Risks shifting adaptation burden onto individuals while reducing employer/government responsibility
Training effectiveness and labor market recognition gaps persist
precedents: Singapore's SkillsFuture provides citizens 25+ with S$500 credit toward 7,000+ courses
May 2024 Level-Up Programme added S$4,000 for 40+ workers
Mid-Career Training Allowance (May 2025) covers 50% income up to S$3,000 monthly for full-time training

policies.title: Vocational Training & Apprenticeships
policies.summary: Expanded technical education and apprenticeships for skilled trades resilient to automation.
policies.core_mechanism: Programs combining classroom instruction with structured on-the-job learning prepare workers for skilled occupations resistant to AI automation while meeting infrastructure demand created by AI deployment.
pros: Develops workers for automation-resistant trades with strong demand
Produces job-ready graduates without requiring four-year degrees
Reaches underserved populations with high completion rates
Creates employment aligned with AI infrastructure buildout
Tech companies investing directly in pipeline support
cons: Private sector participation inconsistent
Vocational pathways stigmatized relative to university education
Apprenticeships designed for young entrants, not mid-career displaced workers
Earnings during apprenticeship may not be financially viable for career changers
Current expansion efforts remain insufficient relative to projected demand
precedents: Germany's dual vocational system with 50-70% youth participation
Google's $10 million electrician training initiative targeting 100,000 new electricians
Microsoft-NABTU partnership (January 2026) strengthening trades apprenticeships for data center construction

policies.title: Token Taxes
policies.summary: Usage-based surcharges on AI model inference creating automatic revenue growth with AI adoption.
policies.core_mechanism: Usage-based surcharges applied to tokens generated by AI models at point of sale, leveraging existing commercial billing infrastructure from providers like OpenAI and Anthropic, with cloud compute providers serving as intermediaries for verification and tax collection.
pros: Captures tax revenue in consumer nations rather than only producer nations
Leverages existing billing infrastructure
Consumption-based approach rather than firm-based
Enforceable through current compute governance systems
Establishes principle that digital value taxed where consumed
cons: Risk of retaliation from US and China where major AI companies headquartered
Could slow AI adoption by raising service prices
May incentivize firms to relocate to favorable tax jurisdictions
Cascading effects if applied to business-to-business transactions
Requires exemptions to avoid production chain impacts
precedents: Digital Services Taxes in France, UK, and Italy on digital company revenues
US federal and state per-unit and percentage-based taxes on telephone and mobile services collected through carrier billing

policies.title: Global Corporate Tax
policies.summary: Higher effective tax rates on the largest multinational enterprises through coordinated global frameworks.
policies.core_mechanism: A coordinated international tax regime applying a global minimum tax rate (currently 15% under OECD's Pillar Two) to multinational enterprises above revenue thresholds, with complementary rules allocating residual profits to market jurisdictions rather than low-tax havens.
pros: Addresses tax base erosion as AI shifts value to capital
Captures disproportionate gains concentrated among technology firms
Reduces profit-shifting to low-tax jurisdictions
Over 145 countries committed to framework
cons: Coordination challenges undermine effectiveness
Unilateral increases risk capital flight
Large tech firms wield significant political influence blocking reforms
US exemption weakens universality
35-40% of multinational profits still shifted to tax havens despite reforms
precedents: OECD BEPS framework adopted by 145+ countries with Pillar One and Two commitments
EU Minimum Tax Directive implemented by 22 of 27 member states as of 2025
38+ countries imposed digital services taxes on foreign tech companies
US secured side-by-side arrangement at 14% rate on worldwide-blended basis

policies.title: Wealth Taxes
policies.summary: An annual tax on accumulated net assets rather than income.
policies.core_mechanism: A levy on net asset value (assets minus liabilities) rather than income flows, designed to capture unrealized capital gains and concentrated wealth that conventional income taxes miss, particularly relevant for AI-driven wealth accrual through equity appreciation.
pros: Captures unrealized gains escaping conventional income taxes
Addresses wealth concentration from AI-driven equity appreciation
Switzerland demonstrates stable revenue generation (≈1% GDP)
Dual income-wealth structure increases evasion difficulty
Avoids liquidity constraints through in-kind share issuance
cons: Valuation challenges for private businesses, intellectual property, and art
Administrative burden
Capital flight risk without international coordination
France repealed its wealth tax citing capital flight and administrative costs
Wealthy individuals have resources to lobby against, relocate to avoid, or structure assets to minimize taxes
precedents: Switzerland maintains cantonal wealth taxes for decades with high compliance
Norway levies annual net wealth taxes
Spain implements wealth taxation
France repealed ISF in 2017 due to capital flight concerns
Warren's Ultra-Millionaire Tax proposal targets top 0.1% with 2-6% rates, projected $3.75T revenue over ten years

policies.title: Consumption Taxes
policies.summary: Broad-based taxes on spending that maintain revenue as labor income declines.
policies.core_mechanism: Levied on spending rather than income or wealth, collected at point of transaction by businesses throughout supply chain or at final sale, making them difficult to evade since spending is observable.
pros: Maintains fiscal base when labor's income share falls
Harder to evade than income taxes
Generates automatic revenue growth with AI adoption
175 countries operate VAT systems successfully
cons: Regressivity places disproportionate burden on lower-income households
Politically unpopular policy change
Digital and cross-border transactions create enforcement gaps
Visible tax that requires infrastructure updates
precedents: OECD data shows 175 countries operate VAT generating average 20.8% of tax revenue
US relies on state/local sales taxes (~32% of collections)
EU adopted VAT in Digital Age (ViDA) package in 2025 for real-time invoicing

policies.title: Automation/Robot Taxes
policies.summary: Taxes that remove fiscal advantages for automation or directly levy AI and robotic deployment.
policies.core_mechanism: Automation taxes target labor-replacing automation by removing preferential tax treatment or directly levying robot/AI deployment. Most tax systems favor capital over labor through deductions, depreciation, and R&D credits, making automation cheaper than employment. These taxes aim to prevent so-so automation exploiting tax arbitrage and could fund worker retraining.
pros: Restores tax neutrality between labor and capital investment
Prevents wasteful automation motivated by tax advantages
Generates revenue for worker retraining and social safety nets
Addresses tax code asymmetry favoring automation
cons: No consensus on defining automation for tax purposes
Firms will invest in circumventing arbitrary boundaries
Risks discouraging beneficial productivity-enhancing automation
Difficult to distinguish so-so from valuable automation in advance
precedents: South Korea (2017) reduced tax credits for automation equipment, resulting in decreased automation investment and increased employment per Kang, Lee, and Quach (2024)
European Parliament rejected robot tax proposal (February 2017) citing innovation concerns

policies.title: AI Equity Taxation
policies.summary: Taxes on AI companies paid via newly-issued equity stakes rather than cash, giving the public both dividend income and a governance voice in AI firms.
policies.core_mechanism: Companies satisfy tax obligations through newly-issued equity dilution rather than cash payments, with stakes held by sovereign wealth funds, public trusts, or stewardship vehicles that collect dividends and exercise shareholder governance rights.
pros: Captures value during high-growth phases when firms report minimal taxable profits
Provides public ownership stake proportional to firms' economic impact
Enables governance participation in consequential AI decisions
Generates revenue streams beyond traditional taxation
cons: Virtually no historical implementation as a fiscal instrument
Raises questions about taxation versus nationalization boundaries
Valuation difficulties for private firms (which include major AI companies)
Uncertain firm and investor responses to progressive dilution
precedents: Clearview AI settlement: 23% equity stake compensation to class-action members
CalPERS public pension fund model for fractional ownership without full control
Bernie Sanders proposal for one-time 50% equity tax on largest AI companies

policies.title: Universal Basic Capital / Equity
policies.summary: Direct ownership stakes in AI infrastructure and the broader economy distributed to all citizens.
policies.core_mechanism: Distributes ownership stakes in productive assets directly to citizens rather than relying solely on wages or government transfers. Takes forms such as publicly seeded investment funds, baby bonds, direct equity stakes in AI infrastructure, or compute capacity allocations. Citizens' stakes appreciate alongside assets, enabling returns to scale with economic growth without requiring ongoing political negotiation.
pros: Broadens capital ownership before concentration becomes entrenched
Returns scale automatically with economic growth
Structurally resilient regardless of which firms or technologies dominate
Provides predistributive approach rather than relying on redistribution
cons: Requires substantial initial capital funding or mandatory corporate contributions
Decades-long maturation timeline makes it generational rather than near-term response
Displaced workers may sell stakes cheaply, concentrating ownership
Difficult governance questions about asset selection, diversification, withdrawal rights, and political interference prevention
precedents: Connecticut Baby Bonds (2021) provides $3,200 investments for Medicaid-eligible children, yielding approximately $10,000-$11,000 by age 18
MAGA program (2025) proposes $1,000 accounts for post-2025 births
Mondragon Corporation demonstrates worker-ownership model redistributing profits and retraining within cooperative structure

policies.title: Sovereign Wealth Funds
policies.summary: State-owned investment vehicles for AI infrastructure and upstream supply chains.
policies.core_mechanism: State-owned funds that invest in domestic AI infrastructure, take equity stakes in AI companies, and capture AI-driven economic gains for the public treasury without relying solely on taxation.
pros: Finances capital-intensive AI infrastructure private sector may avoid
Provides state financial upside and governance influence over consequential AI systems
Converts private wealth creation into public revenue for services and safety nets
Successful precedents like Norway and Alaska demonstrate viability
cons: Concentration risk if single sector underperforms
Governance challenges balancing political pressure with sound investment decisions
Inherent conflict of interest when state both regulates and holds equity in AI firms
Tension between financial returns and strategic national capacity goals
International compliance voluntary with variable adherence
precedents: Alaska Permanent Fund (1976) converting oil revenues to diversified assets
Norway's Government Pension Fund Global (1990) as foundational model
Temasek achieving 7% annual returns over 20 years
Saudi Arabia's $40 billion AI allocation
France's €10 billion Bpifrance AI ecosystem investment

policies.title: Data Compensation
policies.summary: Payments to individuals for the use of their data in training AI models.
policies.core_mechanism: Formalize data contributions as economically valuable by compensating individuals, creators, and communities when their personal data, content, or intellectual property trains AI systems through mechanisms like direct royalties, data dividends, or data trusts.
pros: Provides economic justice for data contributors
Enables displaced workers to retain connection to value chain
Has direct causal logic avoiding redistribution debates
Treats AI surplus as collective product built on shared assets
cons: Measuring individual contributions to billion-point datasets is technically difficult
Per-person payments may be negligible
Data provenance tracking and enforcement challenges
Intermediaries may capture proceeds instead of creators
Restrictive requirements could slow AI development or concentrate advantage among incumbents
precedents: HarperCollins-Microsoft deal paying authors $2,500 per book (2025)
Adobe and Shutterstock creator funds providing annual bonuses
Reddit's $200+ million licensing deals with Google and OpenAI
Ocean Protocol and Solid Project blockchain infrastructure for data monetization

policies.title: Windfall Clause
policies.summary: Voluntary commitments by AI firms to share profits above an extraordinary threshold.
policies.core_mechanism: Voluntary, ex-ante commitments by AI firms to donate a substantial portion of future profits if they exceed a certain threshold. Below threshold, normal operations; above it, escalating profit shares directed to public benefit through donations, public funds, or equity contributions.
pros: Avoids negotiating redistribution after extreme concentration occurs
Pre-commits firms while competing and outcomes uncertain
Costs firms nothing near-term, easier to sign credibly
Addresses scenarios conventional taxation cannot handle
cons: Enforceability challenges with voluntary commitments subject to renegotiation
Depends on courts facing intense pressure from economically dominant firms
Profit-based mechanisms inherit corporate tax evasion problems
Vulnerable to management/ownership changes
precedents: Advance Market Commitments in vaccine development (legally binding pledges before product existence)
Anthropic's Public Benefit Corporation structure with Long-Term Benefit Trust (permits board to balance public benefit with shareholder interests)

policies.title: Intellectual Property Reform
policies.summary: Adapted copyright and patent frameworks for AI training data and AI-generated outputs.
policies.core_mechanism: IP reform addresses legal frameworks governing AI system inputs and outputs. Key questions include whether creators should receive compensation when copyrighted works train AI models, and who owns AI-generated content. Proposals range from expanding fair use exceptions to mandatory licensing schemes modeled on music industry collective rights organizations to transparency requirements.
pros: Enables creator compensation for training data use
Creates clarity on AI output ownership
Establishes transparent disclosure of training sources
Music industry collective licensing provides scalable aggregation model
Balances developer access with creator rights protection
cons: Fragmented international legal landscape creates developer uncertainty
Opt-out mechanisms burden creators with monitoring
Opt-in mechanisms could make assembling training data prohibitively difficult
Courts reaching contradictory conclusions on fair use
Aggregation challenge across millions of individual claims
precedents: Music industry collective licensing (ASCAP, BMI, SESAC model)
Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence (Feb 2025) rejected fair use for AI training
Kadrey v. Meta and Bartz v. Anthropic (June 2025) found transformative fair use
EU Digital Single Market Directive opt-out exceptions
EU AI Act training data summary requirements

policies.title: Regulatory Agencies
policies.summary: Dedicated bodies with technical capacity to monitor high-risk AI systems.
policies.core_mechanism: AI regulatory agencies are public institutions that monitor and evaluate AI deployment in high-risk domains, with functions including licensing systems before deployment, auditing for bias and safety, investigating harms, and maintaining technical expertise to keep pace with evolving technology.
pros: Enables preemptive identification of workforce displacement
Compels disclosure of deployment timelines and capability assessments
Conducts scenario planning for labor market impacts
Stress-tests social safety nets against disruption
cons: Regulatory agencies struggle to build analytical capacity matching AI advancement speed
Technical talent recruitment difficult due to private sector compensation
Forecasting adoption rates and impact involves inherent uncertainty
Risk of regulatory capture if dependent on industry expertise
precedents: Congressional Office of Technology Assessment (1972-1995) provided objective analysis of emerging technology impacts
Federal Reserve stress tests model scenario planning against economic shocks

policies.title: AI Liability
policies.summary: Legal frameworks assigning financial responsibility for AI-caused harms.
policies.core_mechanism: AI liability frameworks determine who bears legal and financial responsibility when AI systems cause harm, allocating responsibility across developers, deployers, users, and potentially AI systems themselves to balance innovation with compensation for impacted people.
pros: Stronger liability regimes incentivize investment in safety and human oversight
Mandatory insurance explicitly prices harm risk
Creates mechanism for displaced workers to recover value
Shifts efficiency gains distribution
cons: Opacity of AI causation advantages defendants
Strict liability risks chilling investment or pushing development to weaker jurisdictions
Piecemeal litigation reflects high-profile harms over diffuse economic displacement
AI fits poorly into existing legal categories
precedents: EU AI Liability Directive (2022) proposed reversed burden of proof for high-risk systems but was scrapped in 2025 work programme
US expanded product liability in 1970s but treated software as services rather than products

policies.title: Legal Economic Personhood
policies.summary: Legal recognition of AI systems as taxable entities with financial obligations.
policies.core_mechanism: AI legal economic personhood would establish artificial intelligence systems as independent economic actors capable of owning assets, entering contracts, paying taxes, and bearing liability—similar to how corporations function as legal entities despite lacking consciousness.
pros: Enables direct taxation of AI-generated wealth at source
Establishes clear legal entity for liability claims
Addresses administrative workability when ownership chains become attenuated
Promotes economic efficiency through property rights and contract capabilities
cons: Could function as liability shield if AI entities structured with minimal assets
Lacks governance structures comparable to corporate boards and fiduciary duties
Requires substantial legal framework changes
Faces political and normative resistance
precedents: Corporations possess property rights and legal standing without consciousness
Trusts and estates function as taxable legal entities
New Zealand's Whanganui River granted legal personhood for environmental protection
India's Ganges River similarly recognized as legal entity

policies.title: Public Utility Regulation
policies.summary: Common carrier and universal access obligations applied to AI infrastructure and services.
policies.core_mechanism: Government oversight of frontier AI systems and compute infrastructure similar to electricity or telecommunications, imposing non-discriminatory access, regulated pricing, reliability standards, and transparency requirements to prevent monopolistic control of essential services.
pros: Prevents monopolistic pricing and exclusionary access
Distributes AI benefits more broadly
Ensures service stability
Reduces concentration of AI capabilities among wealthy actors
Addresses market failures in essential services
cons: Difficulty defining what constitutes essential AI
Heterogeneous and rapidly evolving capabilities resist standardization
Regulation may slow beneficial capability advancement
Risks entrenching incumbent providers
Tension between stability requirements and innovation
precedents: Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 established just and reasonable rates for railroads
FCC regulates ISPs as common carriers under Title II of Communications Act

policies.title: Regulatory Markets
policies.summary: Competitive markets of licensed private regulators selling compliance services to AI companies.
policies.core_mechanism: Governments define regulatory outcomes while licensed private regulators compete to develop and sell compliance services to AI companies, with license revocation as enforcement mechanism.
pros: Addresses technical expertise deficit in government
Introduces competitive innovation in compliance methods
Enables outcome-based enforcement of complex principles
Aligns private regulator interests with public outcomes through license threat
cons: Risk of regulatory capture and race-to-bottom competition on cost
Inadequate government oversight capacity
Difficulty verifying diffuse economic harms
Historical precedents show private certification failures (credit ratings 2008, Boeing 737 MAX)
precedents: Credit rating agencies failed due to inadequate government oversight and deliberate shielding from liability
FAA delegation to Boeing contributed to 737 MAX crashes
Product safety bodies (UL, TÜV) provide successful precedent
Professional licensing regimes demonstrate working model

policies.title: Fiscal Automatic Stabilizers
policies.summary: Pre-legislated fiscal rules that activate automatically when economic indicators cross defined thresholds.
policies.core_mechanism: Fiscal mechanisms that expand government spending or reduce taxes during downturns without requiring new legislation. Trigger-based designs activate proportionally to disruption severity, reducing political lag and enabling smooth scaling from modest adjustment support to broader income protection.
pros: Activates quickly without waiting for new legislation
Reduces political lag historically delaying fiscal action
Scales smoothly with disruption severity
Pre-commitment reduces real-time negotiation
Proven track record in advanced economies offsetting ~60% of income shocks
cons: Existing stabilizers designed for cyclical recessions, not structural displacement
May be undersized or too slow for AI-driven job losses
Measurement challenges if displacement occurs through wage erosion or labor force exit rather than formal unemployment
Difficult to target sectoral disruptions rolling out over years
precedents: Germany's Kurzarbeit saved ~400,000 jobs during 2008 crisis
OECD automatic stabilizers offset average 60% of household income shock across 23 member countries
Claudia Sahm's direct payment proposal using 0.50pp unemployment threshold

policies.title: Monetary Policy Responses
policies.summary: Adaptations to central bank frameworks to manage AI-driven disruptions to prices and employment.
policies.core_mechanism: Central banks adjust interest rates, money supply, and lending facilities to influence borrowing and spending. AI disruptions create challenges: rapid productivity gains may require recognizing shifts in real time to avoid setting rates incorrectly, while AI-powered pricing algorithms could accelerate price adjustments faster than traditional models assume, and simultaneous employment displacement alongside output growth creates conflicting policy pressures.
pros: Leverages existing central bank tools
Allows recognition of productivity-driven growth (as in 1990s IT boom)
Provides economy-wide demand management
Enables adaptive policy frameworks
cons: Blunt instrument unable to target specific displaced workers or sectors
Aggregate indicators may mask severe localized disruption
Difficulty measuring output gap with AI-driven change
Risk of deflationary pressure below effective zero-rate bound
Institutional mandates may become misaligned with structural transformation needs
precedents: Federal Reserve's 1990s productivity response under Greenspan kept rates lower than models predicted, supporting expansion
Bank of Japan's decades-long struggle with deflation despite pioneering unconventional tools illustrates risks when technology coincides with structural demand weakness

policies.title: Antitrust Law
policies.summary: Competition enforcement to prevent monopolistic control over essential AI infrastructure.
policies.core_mechanism: Antitrust law prevents dominant firms from leveraging control over essential AI infrastructure to stifle competition. It targets excessive market concentration, anti-competitive behavior, and abuse of dominant positions, focusing on vertical integration, acqui-hires, exclusive partnerships, and technical lock-ins that could concentrate gatekeeping power among a few incumbents.
pros: Prevents economic gatekeeping by dominant firms
Ensures modular AI stack
Distributes AI benefits more broadly
Enables startup competition
Encourages diverse business models beyond automation-focused approaches
cons: Regulatory processes move slower than AI market dynamics
Difficulty demonstrating consumer harm in zero-price service markets
Fragmentation could slow capable system development
Traditional antitrust tools struggle with multi-layer technology products
precedents: DOJ vs. Google established exclusive distribution deals violate antitrust law
United States v. Microsoft forced unbundling of Internet Explorer from Windows to prevent monopoly protection

policies.title: Public Benefit Corporations
policies.summary: Corporate structures requiring directors to balance societal benefit alongside shareholder returns.
policies.core_mechanism: A PBC is a legal structure allowing directors to consider stakeholder interests beyond shareholders—workers, communities, and the public—when making decisions. Directors receive explicit legal protection under the business judgment rule when prioritizing mission-driven objectives, enabling AI companies to conduct safety testing, decline risky deployments, or invest in alignment research without shareholder litigation risk.
pros: Provides legal protection for directors prioritizing safety over short-term profits
Embeds public benefit commitments into corporate DNA
Enables deliberate product restraint without breach-of-duty claims
Proven adoption by established companies like Patagonia and Kickstarter
cons: Legal protections remain untested in court regarding safety-shareholder conflicts
Capital market pressures may constrain actual implementation
Risk of amoral drift as mission commitments erode over time
Voluntary adoption means non-compliant firms face no mandate
Corporate governance alone insufficient against superstakeholder profit incentives
precedents: Anthropic incorporated as Delaware PBC with Long-Term Benefit Trust (September 2023)
OpenAI completed transformation to PBC structure (October 2025)
Patagonia, Kickstarter, Allbirds adopted PBC model
Thousands of B Corps certified globally

policies.title: Fiduciary Mandates
policies.summary: Legal duties requiring AI developers to act in users' and society's interests.
policies.core_mechanism: Legal duties of loyalty, care, and confidentiality imposed on AI developers and deployers, requiring them to act in users' and society's interests rather than solely maximizing profit.
pros: Converts voluntary ethical commitments into enforceable legal obligations
Prevents design of addictive systems that exploit asymmetric information
Requires ongoing monitoring for downstream harms
Establishes accountability for worker displacement and data misuse
cons: Translating one-to-one professional duties to multi-user systems creates ambiguity
Conflicting interests among millions of users difficult to reconcile
Undefined user interests increases litigation risk that may chill innovation
Conservative framework may discourage beneficial short-term disruptions with long-term gains
precedents: Physicians' Hippocratic obligations and attorney-client duties (centuries of precedent)
SEC's 2019 Regulation Best Interest requires broker-dealers to act in retail customers' best interest
Investment Advisers Act of 1940

policies.title: Public Board Representation
policies.summary: Reserved board seats at AI companies for workers or public interest representatives.
policies.core_mechanism: Companies reserve board seats for directors representing non-shareholder constituencies including workers, public interest advocates, or government appointees, ranging from mandatory codetermination laws to voluntary stakeholder governance structures.
pros: Surfaces information shareholder-aligned boards might underweight (workforce displacement, safety investment adequacy)
Provides internal check on pressure to prioritize speed over caution
Enables formal voice for affected constituencies in strategic decisions
cons: Minority representation may be consistently outvoted or excluded from consequential discussions
Tension between representation and accountability regarding government-appointed directors
Raises conflicts of interest and regulatory independence questions
precedents: Germany's Codetermination Act requires half supervisory board seats for workers in companies exceeding 2,000 employees (2021 NBER study found nonexistent or small positive effects on firm performance)
Mandatory codetermination exists in Austria, Denmark, Finland, Norway, Sweden with representation typically one-third to one-half
Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust appoints trustees with fiduciary duties to AI safety mission rather than profit maximization

policies.title: Public Ownership
policies.summary: Non-controlling government equity stakes in AI companies and critical technology firms.
policies.core_mechanism: Governments acquire equity stakes in strategically important companies, securing governance rights and financial returns without operational control. This includes board observer seats, information access, veto power over foreign acquisitions or corporate control changes, and leverage to negotiate workforce commitments, domestic manufacturing requirements, or safety standards.
pros: Provides real-time visibility into capability development and corporate strategy
Captures AI-driven wealth creation for public treasury
Creates leverage to negotiate public interest conditions
Addresses accountability gap in frontier AI firms operating with national security significance
cons: Creates inherent conflict of interest between investment protection and regulatory enforcement
Can distort competition if government-backed firms receive preferential treatment
Selection problem risks exposing taxpayers to poor financial decisions
Boundary between minority influence and state control can blur over time, especially with accumulated stakes
precedents: U.S. acquired 9.9% non-voting stake in Intel (August 2025, $8.9B) with warrant for additional 5%
Pentagon purchased $400M stake in MP Materials (rare-earth producer)
Department of Energy acquired 5% stakes in Lithium Americas and Thacker Pass joint venture
Germany's KfW used strategic investments to block foreign acquisitions of critical infrastructure

policies.title: Procurement Policies
policies.summary: Public purchasing rules that shape AI markets and attach public benefit obligations.
policies.core_mechanism: Government procurement policies determine how public agencies purchase, deploy, and manage AI systems. Because governments are among the largest technology purchasers, these decisions influence which companies grow, which capabilities develop, what standards become industry norms, and whether AI serves citizens or vendors. Procurement frameworks set terms around transparency, interoperability, data ownership, bias testing, security, and monitoring.
pros: Shapes markets toward public interest goals
Leverages government purchasing power to drive responsible AI deployment
Can steer innovation toward worker-complementary tools
Establishes industry norms for transparency and accountability
Accelerates firms aligned with public benefit objectives
cons: Complex requirements may entrench large vendors with compliance infrastructure
Procurement power can be coercive and punish companies for policy positions
Government dependence on foreign AI providers may invert power dynamics
'Shadow AI' through pilots and free tools bypasses formal oversight
precedents: DARPA's ARPANET research funding seeded internet development (1969)
Medicare/Medicaid EHR programs distributed $27 billion driving health IT adoption
NASA Apollo Program imposed stringent reliability requirements enhancing aerospace competition and safety
Trump administration designated Anthropic supply chain risk over autonomous weapons provisions

policies.title: Public-Private Partnerships
policies.summary: Structured government-private collaborations to co-finance and co-govern AI infrastructure.
policies.core_mechanism: Formal contractual arrangements where governments and private firms share responsibility for financing, building, and operating AI-critical infrastructure (data centers, compute clusters, energy generation, connectivity). Governments provide land, permitting, subsidies, and demand guarantees; private firms contribute technical expertise, operational capacity, and co-investment.
pros: Accelerates infrastructure buildout by combining public capital with private expertise
Prevents concentration of access among dominant firms
Enables nondiscriminatory access requirements and workforce development obligations
Spreads capital burden across both sectors
cons: Information asymmetries favor private partners in contract negotiation
Risk allocation typically lopsided with government absorbing downside
Renegotiation leverage shifts to private partners over 10-30 year terms
Technological change may render fixed contracts obsolete
Public support for private entities must be accompanied by public interest expectations
precedents: America's AI Action Plan streamlines permitting for public-private collaboration on data centers and energy infrastructure
TSMC (1986) structured as hybrid venture with Taiwan's Executive Yuan holding 48.3% equity alongside private investors

policies.title: Benefit-Sharing
policies.summary: International frameworks distributing AI's economic gains to lower-income countries.
policies.core_mechanism: Benefit-sharing encompasses mechanisms to distribute AI economic gains beyond leading countries and companies through resource sharing (compute, datasets, expertise), access sharing (AI systems for global public goods), and financial redistribution (dividend funds, development finance, direct transfers).
pros: Prevents concentration of AI wealth in wealthy nations
Reduces geopolitical instability
Enables participation in governance by excluded countries
Provides access to AI tools for adaptation to displacement effects
cons: Leading countries and companies lack incentives to voluntarily share
Sharing frontier capabilities risks dual-use system proliferation
Achieving multilateral coordination difficult under current geopolitics
Resource sharing without capacity-building creates dependency rather than self-sufficiency
precedents: Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit Sharing (genetic resources)
Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria (pooled international financing model)
COVAX Facility (vaccine equity challenges)

policies.title: Global Dividend Funds
policies.summary: International mechanisms distributing AI-generated surplus as payments to individuals worldwide.
policies.core_mechanism: International institution accumulating ownership stakes in AI-driven economic activity and converting returns into direct payments to individuals globally, funded through equity stakes, taxation, or voluntary commitments by governments and firms.
pros: Addresses cross-border displacement effects that national schemes cannot capture
Channels concentrated AI gains from developed nations to countries bearing disruption costs without sharing returns
Creates economic participation floor independent of government fiscal capacity
Builds on proven dividend mechanisms (Alaska, Cherokee Nations, Macau)
cons: No precedent for global-scale individual distribution across national boundaries
Requires unprecedented multilateral agreement and governance structure
Identity verification and payment infrastructure challenges in weak institutional contexts
Per-person payments may be modest despite large absolute fund size
Raises accountability questions across diverse political systems
precedents: Alaska Permanent Fund (oil revenues, $3,284 per resident in 2022)
Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians casino dividend ($9,000+ annually since 1996)
Macau Wealth Partaking Scheme (gaming revenues, ~$750-$1,250 annually)

policies.title: Restructuring International Organizations
policies.summary: New or reformed international bodies for AI governance and standard-setting.
policies.core_mechanism: Creating new AI-specific bodies or adapting existing organizations to establish coordinated international governance frameworks capable of setting standards, monitoring compliance, and ensuring AI development serves global interests rather than narrow national or corporate ones.
pros: Addresses fragmented governance landscape
Coordinates responses to labor displacement and profit shifting
Creates forums for shared minimum standards
Can facilitate equitable distribution of AI's gains across borders
Models exist from ILO, FSB, and IAEA for reference
cons: Powerful AI-developing nations lack incentive to accept constraining governance
Developing countries distrust existing institutions reflecting wealthy nations' interests
Institutional design timelines may lag behind AI development pace
Enforcement mechanisms historically weak in comparable bodies
precedents: International Labour Organization sets labor standards across borders but faces weak enforcement
Financial Stability Board coordinates national regulators without supranational authority, relying on peer review
International Atomic Energy Agency combines promotion with safety oversight, though nuclear technology differs fundamentally from AI in concentration and detectability

policies.title: Development Banks
policies.summary: Multilateral development bank financing for AI infrastructure with benefit-sharing conditions attached.
policies.core_mechanism: MDBs finance regional compute hubs, connectivity, and training while attaching loan conditions requiring benefit-sharing, labor support, data sovereignty, and environmental standards to shape AI governance.
pros: Mobilizes capital at scale for underserved regions
Embeds public interest requirements into AI infrastructure
Coordinates cross-country investment
Accepts risks private investors avoid
Creates mechanism for accountability before regulation becomes necessary
cons: MDB processes are slow and bureaucratic
Timeline mismatches with rapidly evolving technology
Recipient countries face absorptive capacity constraints
AI investments may strain public finances with uncertain returns
precedents: MDB climate finance committed record $125 billion in 2023 with common result-tracking methodologies (WRI)
G20 Roadmap endorsed November 2024 for enhanced MDB coordination (IADB)
AfDB-Intel partnership targeting 3 million Africans for AI skills training (AfDB)
EIB €70 billion commitment 2025-2027 for disruptive tech projects (EIB Group)

policies.title: National Dividend Funds
policies.summary: Public ownership stakes whose profits are distributed as cash payments to all citizens.
policies.core_mechanism: State-owned investment vehicle acquiring equity in high-value industries, distributing resulting returns directly to citizens as regular cash payments, sustained by investment returns rather than tax appropriations.
pros: Ensures AI-driven productivity gains flow to households automatically
Scales naturally with the magnitude of AI windfalls
Fiscally self-sustaining once capitalized
Less vulnerable to political cycles than tax-appropriated programs
Provides every citizen an ownership stake in economic transformation
cons: Requires large upfront public investment or mandatory equity contributions, neither politically straightforward
Governance demands institutional independence comparable to central banks
Concentrated holdings in AI sector create vulnerability to technology downturns when citizen support is most needed
Decades of patient accumulation may be necessary
precedents: Alaska's Permanent Fund distributing annual dividends since 1982, with residents receiving $3,284 in 2022
Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians casino dividend program distributing at least $9,000 yearly since 1996
Macau's Wealth Partaking Scheme providing annual handouts to all residents

policies.title: Universal Basic Income
policies.summary: Unconditional, regular cash payments to all citizens regardless of employment status.
policies.core_mechanism: Periodic cash payments distributed universally without means testing or work requirements, providing an income floor to cushion AI-driven job displacement and maintain consumer demand in an automated economy.
pros: Reduces bureaucratic overhead compared to means-tested programs
Eliminates stigma and eligibility gaps in safety nets
Provides immediate income security for displaced workers
Maintains aggregate consumer demand
Supports retraining and entrepreneurship
Simpler administration than targeted welfare
cons: Enormously expensive—$12,000 per U.S. adult annually costs over $3 trillion
Requires unprecedented taxation or fundamental restructuring of transfer programs
Addresses symptoms rather than productive capital ownership
May undermine social cohesion by severing contribution-reward link
Experimental evidence shows 4.1 percentage point reduction in labor participation
precedents: GiveDirectly delivered $126M to 200,000+ recipients across 12 African countries in 2024, with one-time $1,000 transfers generating 2.5x economic activity in rural Kenya
South Korea's Gyeonggi Province youth dividend increased happiness while boosting small business revenues by 27%

policies.title: Tax Credit Expansion
policies.summary: Scaling-up tax credit programs to reach a broader set of workers.
policies.core_mechanism: Tax credit expansion uses the existing tax system to deliver targeted financial support to workers and families. Credits can be adjusted by increasing generosity, broadening income eligibility, or making them fully refundable. Earned income credits act as wage subsidies, child tax credits reduce family poverty, and training credits offset skill acquisition costs.
pros: Uses established tax infrastructure enabling rapid scaling
Demonstrated effectiveness (2021 CTC expansion cut child poverty ~40%)
Preserves work incentives by closing wage-market gaps
Creates negative marginal tax rates at low income levels
Flexible tool adjustable to different AI scenarios
cons: Ineffective for those unable to find work
Annual tax filing creates timing delays unless converted to advance payments
Advance payment structures introduce overpayment risks
Targeting precision increases complexity and compliance burdens
UK's Working Tax Credit experienced persistent overpayment and clawback problems
precedents: U.S. EITC (1975) lifted an estimated 5.6 million people from poverty in 2018
2021 CTC expansion achieved 25% reduction in child poverty
UK Working Tax Credit (2003-2025) increased lone parent employment but created overpayment issues
South Korea's EITC reaches one in four households with positive employment effects
